claim: The iris controls the level of retinal illumination by controlling pupil diameter.
source: The iris controls the level of retinal illumination by controlling pupil diameter.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical and physiological knowledge about iris function.

claim: The iris is a site of diverse ophthalmologic diseases.
source: The iris controls the level of retinal illumination by controlling pupil diameter. It is a site of diverse ophthalmologic diseases and it is a potential source of cells for ocular auto-transplantation.
evidence: This is supported by established medical knowledge and literature.

claim: The iris is a potential source of cells for ocular auto-transplantation.
source: It is a site of diverse ophthalmologic diseases and it is a potential source of cells for ocular auto-transplantation.
evidence: This is supported by prior research discussed in the manuscript.

claim: This study defined all of the major cell types in the mouse iris and ciliary body.
source: More specifically, this work has (1) defined all of the major cell types in the mouse iris and ciliary body
evidence: This is supported by the snRNAseq data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two types of iris stromal cells exist in the mouse iris.
source: (2) led to the discovery of two types of iris stromal cells and two types of iris sphincter cells
evidence: This is supported by snRNAseq clustering analysis and marker gene expression patterns shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Two types of iris sphincter cells exist in the mouse iris.
source: (2) led to the discovery of two types of iris stromal cells and two types of iris sphincter cells
evidence: This is supported by snRNAseq clustering analysis and marker gene expression patterns shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Cell type-specific transcriptomes differ between resting and dilated iris states.
source: (3) revealed the differences in cell type-specific transcriptomes in the resting vs. dilated states
evidence: This is supported by comparative snRNAseq analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Antibody and in situ hybridization probes were identified and validated to visualize major iris cell types.
source: (4) identified and validated antibody and in situ hybridization probes that can be used to visualize the major iris cell types.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and ISH data shown throughout Figures 2-5.

claim: Iris dilation causes distortions in nuclear morphology.
source: By immunostaining for specific iris cell types, we have observed and quantified distortions in nuclear morphology associated with iris dilation
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of nuclear length:width ratios shown in Figure 8.

claim: Wnt1-Cre-expressing progenitors contribute to nearly all iris cell types.
source: clarified the neural crest contribution to the iris by showing that Wnt1-Cre-expressing progenitors contribute to nearly all iris cell types
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Sox10-Cre-expressing progenitors contribute only to stromal cells.
source: whereas Sox10-Cre-expressing progenitors contribute only to stromal cells
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: The iris is a thin disc of light-absorbing tissue with a central opening.
source: The iris, a thin disc of light-absorbing tissue with a central opening, is located in front of the lens and divides the eye into anterior and posterior chambers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The iris is located in front of the lens.
source: The iris, a thin disc of light-absorbing tissue with a central opening, is located in front of the lens and divides the eye into anterior and posterior chambers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The iris divides the eye into anterior and posterior chambers.
source: The iris, a thin disc of light-absorbing tissue with a central opening, is located in front of the lens and divides the eye into anterior and posterior chambers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Muscular contraction within the iris controls pupil diameter.
source: Muscular contraction within the iris controls the diameter of the central opening – the pupil – to adjust the amount of light impinging on the retina.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge.

claim: The iris controls the amount of light impinging on the retina.
source: Muscular contraction within the iris controls the diameter of the central opening – the pupil – to adjust the amount of light impinging on the retina.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge.

claim: The iris has been an object of popular and scientific fascination for centuries.
source: The iris has been an object of popular and scientific fascination for centuries, most likely as a consequence of its position as the principal target of gaze fixation in interpersonal encounters, the unconscious responses of the pupil to different psychological states, and the great diversity in iris appearance/pigmentation among humans (Duke-Elder and Wybar, 1961; Larsen and Waters, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by historical literature citations.

claim: The iris is the principal target of gaze fixation in interpersonal encounters.
source: The iris has been an object of popular and scientific fascination for centuries, most likely as a consequence of its position as the principal target of gaze fixation in interpersonal encounters, the unconscious responses of the pupil to different psychological states, and the great diversity in iris appearance/pigmentation among humans (Duke-Elder and Wybar, 1961; Larsen and Waters, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and general knowledge.

claim: The pupil exhibits unconscious responses to different psychological states.
source: The iris has been an object of popular and scientific fascination for centuries, most likely as a consequence of its position as the principal target of gaze fixation in interpersonal encounters, the unconscious responses of the pupil to different psychological states, and the great diversity in iris appearance/pigmentation among humans (Duke-Elder and Wybar, 1961; Larsen and Waters, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and established knowledge.

claim: There is great diversity in iris appearance and pigmentation among humans.
source: The iris has been an object of popular and scientific fascination for centuries, most likely as a consequence of its position as the principal target of gaze fixation in interpersonal encounters, the unconscious responses of the pupil to different psychological states, and the great diversity in iris appearance/pigmentation among humans (Duke-Elder and Wybar, 1961; Larsen and Waters, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and observable human variation.

claim: Some anterior ocular structures are derived from the neural crest via its contribution to the peri-ocular mesenchyme.
source: Lineage tracing experiments in avian embryos provided the first evidence that some anterior ocular structures were derived, at least partially, from the neural crest via its contribution to the peri-ocular mesenchyme (Johnston et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by the cited lineage tracing study.

claim: Neural crest lineage tracing in mice has produced conflicting results regarding iris contribution.
source: Neural crest lineage tracing in mice using Cre-LoxP to mark cells has produced conflicting results, with one laboratory describing no contribution of neural crest cell to the iris with a Wnt1-Cre driver (Gage et al., 2005) and a second laboratory showing neural crest contributions to iris stroma with a P0-Cre driver (Kanakubo et al., 2006; Kikuchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting published studies.

claim: The human pupil exhibits an approximately 4-fold variation in diameter between constricted and dilated states.
source: The human pupil exhibits an ~4-fold variation in diameter between constricted and dilated states (Duke-Elder and Wybar, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: There are extended periods of pupil constriction induced by sunlight during the day under natural conditions.
source: Under natural conditions, there are extended periods of pupil constriction, induced by sunlight during the day, alternating with extended periods of pupil dilation, induced by darkness at night.
evidence: This is based on general physiological knowledge.

claim: There are extended periods of pupil dilation induced by darkness at night under natural conditions.
source: Under natural conditions, there are extended periods of pupil constriction, induced by sunlight during the day, alternating with extended periods of pupil dilation, induced by darkness at night.
evidence: This is based on general physiological knowledge.

claim: Pharmacologic dilation is produced by topical administration of an alpha-adrenergic agonist and/or a muscarinic antagonist.
source: Pharmacologic dilation, produced by topical administration of an alpha-adrenergic agonist and/or a muscarinic antagonist, is widely used in the context of routine ophthalmologic exams and ocular surgery (Paggiarino et al., 1993; Motta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical literature and established medical practice.

claim: Pharmacologic dilation is widely used in routine ophthalmologic exams and ocular surgery.
source: Pharmacologic dilation, produced by topical administration of an alpha-adrenergic agonist and/or a muscarinic antagonist, is widely used in the context of routine ophthalmologic exams and ocular surgery (Paggiarino et al., 1993; Motta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical literature and established medical practice.

claim: Several iris cell types exhibit striking changes in shape in response to constriction and dilation.
source: In response to constriction and dilation, several iris cell types exhibit striking changes in shape and in the arrangement of their plasma membranes and cytoskeletal fibers (Lim and Webber, 1975a).
evidence: This is supported by the cited ultrastructural study.

claim: Several iris cell types exhibit changes in the arrangement of their plasma membranes and cytoskeletal fibers in response to constriction and dilation.
source: In response to constriction and dilation, several iris cell types exhibit striking changes in shape and in the arrangement of their plasma membranes and cytoskeletal fibers (Lim and Webber, 1975a).
evidence: This is supported by the cited ultrastructural study.

claim: There are no known molecular correlates of cellular responses to iris constriction and dilation.
source: At present, there are no known molecular correlates of these cellular responses.
evidence: This represents a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Ten iris cell clusters were identified with Seurat.
source: Ten iris cell clusters were identified with Seurat, and their identities were subsequently assigned by immunostaining and ISH, as described below.
evidence: This is supported by the computational analysis and validation experiments.

claim: The UMAP plot revealed a distinctive distribution of the 10 clusters including a comma shape consisting of iris pigment epithelium and adjacent ciliary body epithelium.
source: A Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plot of the snRNAseq data revealed a distinctive distribution of the 10 clusters (Figure 1B and C): (1) a comma shape, consisting of the iris pigment epithelium (PE) and the adjacent and contiguous ciliary body epithelium (CBE)
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The UMAP plot shows a C-shaped arc in which dilator muscle connects to non-epithelial ciliary body cells on one side and sphincter muscle on the other side.
source: (2) a C-shaped arc in which dilator muscle connects to non-epithelial ciliary body cells on one side and sphincter muscle on the other side
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The UMAP plot shows two widely separated clusters of stromal cells.
source: (3) two widely separated clusters of stromal cells (referred to as stroma 1 and stroma 2)
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The UMAP plot shows small clusters of leukocytes and endothelial cells.
source: (4) small clusters of leukocytes and endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 1C.

claim: UMAP plots are well matched across treatment conditions and independent replicates.
source: UMAP plots are well matched across treatment conditions and independent replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by the supplementary figure showing consistency across samples.

claim: A small shift in the location of the dilator muscle cell cluster occurs upon pupil dilation.
source: with the only visually apparent difference being a small shift in the location of the dilator muscle cell cluster upon pupil dilation.
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dilator muscle is responsive to alpha-adrenergic agonists.
source: For example, classic pharmacologic studies have shown that the dilator muscle is responsive to alpha-adrenergic agonists and the sphincter muscle is responsive to muscarinic agonists.
evidence: This is supported by established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: The sphincter muscle is responsive to muscarinic agonists.
source: For example, classic pharmacologic studies have shown that the dilator muscle is responsive to alpha-adrenergic agonists and the sphincter muscle is responsive to muscarinic agonists.
evidence: This is supported by established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Transcripts coding for the alpha-1A adrenergic receptor (Adra1a) are enriched in the dilator cluster.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, transcripts coding for the alpha-1A adrenergic receptor (Adra1a) are enriched in the dilator cluster
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP expression plot in Figure 1D.

claim: Transcripts coding for muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 3 (Chrm3) are enriched in the sphincter cluster.
source: and transcripts coding for muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 3 (Chrm3) are enriched in the sphincter cluster.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP expression plot in Figure 1D.

claim: The sphincter 2 sub-cluster contains both Adra1a and Chrm3 transcripts.
source: Interestingly, the sub-cluster of sphincter cells closest to the dilator cluster (referred to as the 'sphincter 2' cluster) contains both transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the snRNAseq data analysis.

claim: Sox10 transcripts show high cluster specificity to stroma 1.
source: Other transcripts that show high cluster specificity include transcription factors Sox10 (stroma 1), Tfap2b (stroma 2), and Zic1 (epithelial cells) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP expression plot in Figure 1D.

claim: Tfap2b transcripts show high cluster specificity to stroma 2.
source: Other transcripts that show high cluster specificity include transcription factors Sox10 (stroma 1), Tfap2b (stroma 2), and Zic1 (epithelial cells) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP expression plot in Figure 1D.

claim: Zic1 transcripts show high cluster specificity to epithelial cells.
source: Other transcripts that show high cluster specificity include transcription factors Sox10 (stroma 1), Tfap2b (stroma 2), and Zic1 (epithelial cells) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP expression plot in Figure 1D.

claim: Transcripts coding for titin (Ttn) are restricted to the sphincter 1 cluster.
source: Transcripts coding for the gigantic muscle protein titin (Ttn) are restricted to the most distal sub-cluster of sphincter cells (referred to as the 'sphincter 1' cluster).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP expression plot in Figure 1D.

claim: The mouse iris contains two distinct types of stromal cells.
source: These data indicate that the mouse iris contains two distinct types of stromal cells and three distinct types of smooth muscle cells.
evidence: This is supported by the scatter plot comparisons in Figure 1E showing distinct transcriptome profiles.

claim: The mouse iris contains three distinct types of smooth muscle cells.
source: These data indicate that the mouse iris contains two distinct types of stromal cells and three distinct types of smooth muscle cells.
evidence: This is supported by the scatter plot comparisons in Figure 1E showing distinct transcriptome profiles.

claim: Smooth muscle actin (SMA) is expressed in all three classes of smooth muscle cells.
source: Smooth muscle actin (SMA, the product of the Acta2 gene) is expressed in all three classes of smooth muscle cells (Figure 2C, D and F–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Strands of dilator muscle typically weave in and out of the plane of section in iris cross sections.
source: In iris cross sections, the strands of dilator muscle typically weave in and out of the plane of section (Figure 2B–G), as inferred from SMA immunostaining of iris flat mounts (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is inferred from immunostaining patterns shown in Figure 2.

claim: Multiple markers for sphincter 1 cells localize throughout the pupil-proximal 10-15% of the iris.
source: Multiple markers for sphincter 1 cells – including neuronal pentraxin-2 (Nptx2), NeuN (Rbfox3), catenin-alpha3 (Ctnna3), muscle creatine kinase (Ckm), and titin (Ttn) – localized throughout the pupil-proximal 10–15% of the iris (Figure 2B–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The pupil-proximal 10-15% of the iris coincides with the region of circumferential muscle fibers.
source: This region coincides with the region of circumferential muscle fibers visualized by SMA immunostaining
evidence: This is inferred from comparing marker localization with SMA staining in Figure 2.

claim: Sphincter 1 and sphincter 2 cells are intermingled with each other within the mass of sphincter muscle fibers.
source: implying that sphincter 1 and sphincter 2 cells are intermingled with each other within the mass of sphincter muscle fibers.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization patterns of cell type markers.

claim: Nitric oxide synthase-1 (Nos1) is specifically expressed in dilator muscle.
source: Nitric oxide synthase-1 (Nos1), the NOS isoform enriched in the nervous system and skeletal muscle, is specifically expressed in dilator muscle and localizes in a pattern reciprocal to that of CKM (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Nos1 transcripts localize to dilator muscle.
source: This analysis localized transcripts for Nos1 to dilator muscle, Ttn to sphincter muscle, and myosin heavy chain-11 (Myh11) to both dilator and sphincter muscles (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ttn transcripts localize to sphincter muscle.
source: This analysis localized transcripts for Nos1 to dilator muscle, Ttn to sphincter muscle, and myosin heavy chain-11 (Myh11) to both dilator and sphincter muscles (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Myh11 transcripts localize to both dilator and sphincter muscles.
source: This analysis localized transcripts for Nos1 to dilator muscle, Ttn to sphincter muscle, and myosin heavy chain-11 (Myh11) to both dilator and sphincter muscles (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) transcripts localize to sphincter 1 and sphincter 2 cells.
source: Transcripts coding for synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1), a calcium sensor that regulates neurotransmitter release, localized to sphincter 1 and sphincter 2 cells (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adra1a transcripts are enriched in dilator muscle.
source: As predicted from the UMAP analysis, Adra1a transcripts are enriched in dilator muscle and Chrm3 transcripts are enriched in sphincter muscle (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Chrm3 transcripts are enriched in sphincter muscle.
source: As predicted from the UMAP analysis, Adra1a transcripts are enriched in dilator muscle and Chrm3 transcripts are enriched in sphincter muscle (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Titin connects the Z-disk to the M-band in striated muscle and acts as an elastic element.
source: Titin, the largest member of the mammalian proteome (~27,000 to ~35,000 amino acids, depending on the splice isoform) connects the Z-disk to the M-band in striated muscle and appears to act as an elastic element, responding to muscle tension by progressively unfolding its many small domains (Chauveau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on titin structure and function.

claim: A similar elastic role for titin in sphincter 1 cells appears plausible in light of the 4-fold change in pupil diameter with dilation and constriction.
source: A similar elastic role in the sphincter 1 cells appears plausible in light of the 4-fold change in pupil diameter – and, hence, sphincter muscle length – with dilation and constriction.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on titin's known function and iris mechanics.

claim: The localization of CTNNA3 to sphincter 1 cells represents a structural/cytoskeletal distinction between sphincter and dilator muscle.
source: The localization of CTNNA3 to sphincter 1 cells represents a second structural/cytoskeletal distinction between sphincter and dilator muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression and known function of CTNNA3.

claim: Alpha-catenins heterodimerize with beta-catenins at adherins junctions and regulate actin filament assembly.
source: Alpha-catenins heterodimerize with beta-catenins at adherins junctions and they regulate actin filament assembly, coordinating junctional and cytoskeletal architectures (Takeichi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on alpha-catenin function.

claim: The localization of NeuN, NPTX2, and SYT1 to sphincter cells suggests that gene expression in sphincter cells has a partially neuronal character.
source: The localization to sphincter cells of NeuN, neuronal activity-regulated pentraxin-2 (NPTX2), and synaptotagmin-1 (SYT1) – all of which are enriched in the nervous system – suggests that gene expression in sphincter cells has a partially neuronal character.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of neuron-enriched genes in sphincter cells.

claim: NeuN/RBFOX3 is an RNA-binding protein that regulates differential pre-mRNA splicing.
source: NeuN/RBFOX3 is an RNA-binding protein that regulates differential pre-mRNA splicing (Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2013; Duan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on NeuN function.

claim: NPTX2 is the product of a neuronal immediate-early gene.
source: NPTX2 (formerly NARP), the product of a neuronal immediate-early gene, is an extracellular protein that enhances neurite outgrowth, clusters AMPA receptors, and promotes synaptic plasticity (Tsui et al., 1996; O'Brien et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on NPTX2.

claim: NPTX2 is an extracellular protein that enhances neurite outgrowth, clusters AMPA receptors, and promotes synaptic plasticity.
source: NPTX2 (formerly NARP), the product of a neuronal immediate-early gene, is an extracellular protein that enhances neurite outgrowth, clusters AMPA receptors, and promotes synaptic plasticity (Tsui et al., 1996; O'Brien et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on NPTX2 function.

claim: SYT1 promotes calcium-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion by arresting the SNARE complex in the pre-fusion state under low calcium conditions.
source: SYT1 promotes calcium-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion by arresting the SNARE complex in the pre-fusion state under low calcium conditions and then allowing the SNARE complex to 'zipper up' its alpha helices and promote membrane fusion in high calcium (Zhou et al., 2017; Ramakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on SYT1 mechanism.

claim: In amphibia, birds, fish, and non-primate mammals, pupil diameter is controlled both by a retina-brainstem-sympathetic/parasympathetic-iris smooth muscle circuit and by the intrinsic light sensitivity of the iris musculature.
source: In amphibia, birds, fish, and non-primate mammals, pupil diameter is controlled both by a retina-brainstem-sympathetic/parasympathetic-iris smooth muscle circuit and by the intrinsic light sensitivity of the iris musculature (Douglas, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on comparative pupil control.

claim: The intrinsic light sensitivity pathway in the iris is mediated by melanopsin (OPN4) via activation of PLCB2 and PLCB4 and calcium release by IP3R1.
source: Studies of knockout mice show that the intrinsic pathway is mediated by the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) photopigment melanopsin (OPN4) via activation of phospholipase C-beta2 and beta4 (PLCB2 and PLCB4) and calcium release by inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor 1 (IP3R1) (Xue et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited knockout mouse studies.

claim: Opn4 is the most highly expressed rhodopsin-like gene in the mouse iris.
source: Our transcriptome analysis shows that of all the genes coding for rhodopsin-like proteins in the mouse genome, Opn4 is the most highly expressed in the iris.
evidence: This is supported by the snRNAseq data analysis.

claim: Opn4 is expressed in both dilator and constrictor muscles and in iris PE cells.
source: Interestingly, it is expressed in both dilator and constrictor muscles, and it is also expressed in iris PE cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transcripts for cryptochromes-1 and -2 (Cry1 and Cry2) are widely expressed in the iris.
source: Transcripts for cryptochromes-1 and -2 (Cry1 and Cry2), flavin-based light sensors implicated in circadian rhythms, are also widely expressed in the iris (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Plcb4 is the most abundant PLC isoform in iris smooth muscle.
source: Transcripts for PLC isozymes show multiple PLC isoforms in iris smooth muscle with Plcb4 being the most abundant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The order of importance for IP3 receptors in the iris is IP3R1 >> IP3R2 > IP3R3.
source: The abundances of transcripts for calcium release channels (IP3 receptors [Itpr1, Itpr2, and Itpr3] and ryanodine receptors [Ryr1, Ryr2, and Ryr3]) implies that their order of importance is IP3R1>> IP3 R2> IP3 R3 and RYR3>> RYR2> RYR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from transcript abundance data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The order of importance for ryanodine receptors in the iris is RYR3 >> RYR2 > RYR1.
source: The abundances of transcripts for calcium release channels (IP3 receptors [Itpr1, Itpr2, and Itpr3] and ryanodine receptors [Ryr1, Ryr2, and Ryr3]) implies that their order of importance is IP3R1>> IP3 R2> IP3 R3 and RYR3>> RYR2> RYR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from transcript abundance data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dilator muscles receive adrenergic input principally via ADRA1A.
source: The distribution of adrenergic and muscarinic receptors implies that (1) dilator muscles receive adrenergic input principally via ADRA1A
evidence: This is inferred from receptor expression patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sphincter muscles receive cholinergic input principally via CHRM3.
source: (2) sphincter muscles receive cholinergic input principally via CHRM3 – consistent with the defect in pupil constriction observed in Chrm3 knockout mice (Matsui et al., 2000) – and, to a lesser extent, via CHRM2
evidence: This is inferred from receptor expression patterns and supported by cited knockout mouse data.

claim: Chrm3 knockout mice have a defect in pupil constriction.
source: (2) sphincter muscles receive cholinergic input principally via CHRM3 – consistent with the defect in pupil constriction observed in Chrm3 knockout mice (Matsui et al., 2000) – and, to a lesser extent, via CHRM2
evidence: This is supported by the cited knockout mouse study.

claim: Dilator muscles receive cholinergic input via CHRM2.
source: (3) dilator muscles receive cholinergic input via CHRM2
evidence: This is inferred from receptor expression patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The pharmacology of sphincter 2 cells is intermediate between sphincter 1 and dilator cells.
source: (4) the pharmacology of sphincter 2 cells is intermediate between sphincter 1 and dilator cells because sphincter 2 cells express levels of alpha-adrenergic receptors and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors that are intermediate between those of sphincter 1 and dilator cells (Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from receptor expression patterns shown in the figures.

claim: Stroma 2 cells are sensitive to adrenergic ligands via ADRA1B receptors.
source: The distribution of alpha-adrenergic receptor transcripts also implies that stroma 2 cells are sensitive to adrenergic ligands via ADRA1B receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from receptor expression patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The inner surface of the iris is occupied by the iris PE, which is contiguous with the adjacent CBE.
source: The inner surface of the iris is occupied by the iris PE, which is contiguous with the adjacent CBE (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Transcription factor ZIC1 localizes exclusively to the nuclei of iris PE and CBE.
source: Transcription factor ZIC1 localizes exclusively to the nuclei of these two epithelia (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: OTX1 and OTX2 are expressed in sphincter and dilator muscles in different proportions.
source: OTX1 and OTX2, two highly homologous transcription factors, are expressed in sphincter and dilator muscles (in different proportions) and OTX1 is additionally expressed in iris PE
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and snRNAseq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: OTX1 is additionally expressed in iris PE.
source: OTX1 and OTX2, two highly homologous transcription factors, are expressed in sphincter and dilator muscles (in different proportions) and OTX1 is additionally expressed in iris PE, as seen by immunostaining with an antibody that recognizes both proteins, referred to hereafter as 'OTX' (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The expression of PAX6 closely matches the OTX expression pattern.
source: The expression of PAX6, a master regulator of anterior eye development, closely matches the OTX expression pattern (Figure 4A, C, and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stroma 1 cells express transcription factors Sox10, Tbx1, Pax3, and Tfap2a.
source: The snRNAseq data shows that stroma 1 cells express transcription factors Sox10, Tbx1, Pax3, and Tfap2a
evidence: This is supported by snRNAseq data shown in Figures 1 and 5 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Stroma 2 cells express Pitx2, Glis1, and Tfap2b.
source: whereas stroma 2 cells express Pitx2, Glis1, and Tfap2b (Figures 1D, F, 5A, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by snRNAseq data shown in the figures and supplementary file.

claim: SOX10 and TFAP2B show mutually exclusive localization in nuclei in the outer half of the iris where stromal cells reside.
source: For SOX10 and TFAP2B, these snRNAseq patterns were confirmed by immunostaining of iris flat mounts and sections, which shows their mutually exclusive localization in nuclei in the outer half of the iris, where stromal cells reside (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The iris has a trilayer structure: stromal cells in the outermost layer, dilator muscle in the central layer, and iris PE in the innermost layer.
source: Co-staining of iris sections for SMA or PDGFRA, markers for muscle and stroma 2 cells, respectively, together with SOX10 or TFAP2B, and with DAPI, shows the trilayer iris structure: stromal cells in the outermost layer, dilator muscle in the central layer, and iris PE in the innermost layer (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by multi-marker immunostaining shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Stroma 1 cells express multiple melanogenesis-related genes including Ednrb, Mitf, Dct, Tyrp1, and Tyr.
source: Stroma 1 cells express multiple melanogenesis-related genes, including endothelin receptor beta (Ednrb), microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (Mitf), dopachrome tautomerase (dopachroma delta-isomerase, Dct), tyrosinase-related protein-1 (Tyrp1), and tyrosinase (Tyr)
evidence: This is supported by snRNAseq data.

claim: Stroma 1 cells serve as a secondary site of melanin synthesis in addition to the iris PE.
source: indicating that they serve as a secondary site of melanin synthesis in addition to the principal site of melanin synthesis and accumulation in the iris PE.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of melanogenesis genes in stroma 1 cells.

claim: The murine iris is uniformly tiled by irregularly shaped stellate cells, of which the majority are macrophages and the minority are dendritic cells.
source: The murine iris is uniformly tiled by irregularly shaped stellate cells, of which the majority are macrophages and the minority are dendritic cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: M2 macrophages comprise approximately half of the CD45 population in the iris.
source: The CD206 population (M2 macrophages) comprise approximately half of the CD45 population (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pharmacologically induced pupil dilation reduces the central-to-peripheral width of the mouse iris by approximately 5-fold.
source: In the mouse iris, pharmacologically induced pupil dilation reduces the central-to-peripheral width of the iris by ~5-fold, which produces a back-and-forth folding of nerves and blood vessels (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Iris dilation produces a back-and-forth folding of nerves and blood vessels.
source: In the mouse iris, pharmacologically induced pupil dilation reduces the central-to-peripheral width of the iris by ~5-fold, which produces a back-and-forth folding of nerves and blood vessels (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The transcriptomes of constricted and untreated irises are virtually indistinguishable across all cell types.
source: As noted in connection with Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, the transcriptomes of constricted and untreated irises are virtually indistinguishable across all cell types
evidence: This is supported by high R² values (0.98-0.99) in scatter plot comparisons shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The untreated pupil diameter is relatively small, so pharmacologic constriction produces only a modest additional reduction in diameter.
source: presumably because the untreated pupil diameter is relatively small, so that pharmacologic constriction produces only a modest additional reduction in its diameter.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of transcriptomes between untreated and constricted conditions.

claim: For seven of the ten iris cell types, there was more scatter in the dilated vs. untreated comparison than in the constricted vs. untreated comparison.
source: For seven of the ten iris cell types, there was more scatter in the dilated vs. untreated comparison than in the constricted vs. untreated comparison (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by R² value comparisons shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The dilator muscle showed the largest transcriptome changes with dilation, with R² reducing from 0.991 (constricted vs. untreated) to 0.920 (dilated vs. untreated).
source: The dilator muscle showed the largest transcriptome changes, with a reduction in R2 from 0.991 (constricted vs. untreated) to 0.920 (dilated vs. untreated).
evidence: This is supported by R² value comparisons shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Egr1 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that is an immediate-early response gene in diverse cell types.
source: Egr1, a zinc-finger transcription factor that is an immediate-early response gene in diverse cell types
evidence: This is established knowledge about Egr1 function.

claim: Slc26a4 is a broad-specificity anion exchanger that is expressed in multiple epithelia.
source: Slc26a4, a broad-specificity anion exchanger that is expressed in multiple epithelia
evidence: This is established knowledge about Slc26a4 function.

claim: Tmem158 is a membrane protein of unknown function.
source: and Tmem158, a membrane protein of unknown function (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about Tmem158.

claim: EGR1 is undetectable in untreated iris and is readily detected in the nuclei of the dilator muscle with pupil dilation.
source: Immunostaining for EGR1, ZIC1, and SMA shows that EGR1 is undetectable in untreated iris and is readily detected in the nuclei of the dilator muscle with pupil dilation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The abundances of ZIC1 in iris PE and SMA in muscle cells are unchanged by dilation.
source: The same sections show that the abundances of ZIC1 in iris PE and SMA in muscle cells are unchanged by dilation.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Slc26a4 and Tmem158 transcripts accumulate in dilator muscle with pupil dilation.
source: Similarly, ISH shows the accumulation of Slc26a4 and Tmem158 transcripts in dilator muscle with pupil dilation, whereas the abundance of Adrala transcripts remains unchanged (Figure 7C, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 7C and quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The abundance of Adra1a transcripts remains unchanged with pupil dilation.
source: Similarly, ISH shows the accumulation of Slc26a4 and Tmem158 transcripts in dilator muscle with pupil dilation, whereas the abundance of Adrala transcripts remains unchanged (Figure 7C, quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 7C and quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anks1b, Btg2, Junb, and Pde10a transcripts accumulate in dilator muscle with pupil dilation.
source: Confirming the snRNAseq data, quantification of the ISH signals showed accumulation of Anks1b, Btg2, Junb, and Pde10a transcripts in dilator muscle and Tmem158 transcripts in sphincter muscle with pupil dilation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantified ISH data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tmem158 transcripts accumulate in sphincter muscle with pupil dilation.
source: Confirming the snRNAseq data, quantification of the ISH signals showed accumulation of Anks1b, Btg2, Junb, and Pde10a transcripts in dilator muscle and Tmem158 transcripts in sphincter muscle with pupil dilation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantified ISH data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pde10a codes for a dual cAMP/cGMP phosphodiesterase.
source: Among the transcripts that exhibit increased abundance with pupil dilation, Pde10a, which codes for a dual cAMP/cGMP phosphodiesterase (Soderling et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on Pde10a function.

claim: Pde10a shows the highest fold change with dilation in dilator, sphincter 2, stroma 1, iris PE, CB, and CB epithelial cells.
source: stands out as showing the highest fold change in dilator, sphincter 2, stroma 1, iris PE, CB, CB epithelial cells, and it shows close to the highest fold change in the other iris cell types (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in the figures and supplementary file.

claim: Other cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase transcripts including Pde1c, Pde3b, Pde4d, and Pde7b are upregulated with dilation.
source: Other cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase transcripts – including Pde1c, Pde3b, Pde4d, Pde7b – are also upregulated
evidence: This is supported by differential expression data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Negative regulation of cyclic nucleotide signaling is a general feature of iris dilation.
source: suggesting that negative regulation of cyclic nucleotide signaling is a general feature of iris dilation (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of multiple phosphodiesterase genes.

claim: Btg2 is the second most highly induced transcript in dilator muscle with dilation.
source: In dilator muscle, the second most highly induced transcript is Btg2
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Btg2 induction is specific to dilator muscle.
source: and, unlike Pde10a, Btg2 induction is specific to dilator muscle (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: BTG2 interacts with the CAF1 subunit of the CCR4-NOT complex to promote deadenylation of mRNAs.
source: BTG2 interacts with the CAF1 subunit of the CCR4-NOT complex to promote deadenylation of mRNAs, with effects ranging from countering cardiomyocyte hypertrophy to maintaining T cell quiescence (Mauxion et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008; Masumura et al., 2016; Hwang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on BTG2 function.

claim: BTG2 could play a regulatory role in the iris dilator muscle analogous to its role in cardiac muscle.
source: BTG2 could play a regulatory role in the iris dilator muscle analogous to its role in cardiac muscle.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on BTG2's known function in cardiac muscle.

claim: EGR1 accumulation in the dilator muscle was apparent within 30 min of the onset of dilation.
source: A time course experiment in which irises were harvested 30, 90, or 150 min after the onset of pupil dilation (maintained by hourly instillations of phenylephrine + cyclopentolate eye drops) showed that EGR1 accumulation in the dilator muscle was apparent within 30 min of the onset of dilation and was maintained thereafter with continuous pupil dilation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by time course immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: EGR1 accumulation was maintained with continuous pupil dilation.
source: A time course experiment in which irises were harvested 30, 90, or 150 min after the onset of pupil dilation (maintained by hourly instillations of phenylephrine + cyclopentolate eye drops) showed that EGR1 accumulation in the dilator muscle was apparent within 30 min of the onset of dilation and was maintained thereafter with continuous pupil dilation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by time course immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: At 30 min after dilation onset, there were scattered EGR-1+ cells in the stromal layer, but the numbers of these cells declined at later time points.
source: At the 30 min point, there were also scattered EGR-1+ cells in the stromal layer, but the numbers of these cells declined at later time points (compare Figure 7A and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A and D.

claim: Changes in nuclear morphology alter chromatin organization, gene expression, and intracellular signals.
source: Current evidence suggests that changes in nuclear morphology alter chromatin organization, gene expression, and intracellular signals (Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Lele et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on nuclear mechanobiology.

claim: All cell types except sphincter 1 showed highly significant increases in nuclear elongation with dilation.
source: The nuclear length:width ratio comparison shows no significant changes with dilation in the highly elongated nuclei of sphincter 1 cells (mean length:width ratio ~6). However, all other cell types showed highly significant (p < 0.0001) increases in nuclear elongation with dilation.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The smallest changes in nuclear elongation with dilation were seen with OTX+ nuclei, with mean length:width ratio increasing from approximately 2 to approximately 3.
source: The smallest changes were seen with OTX+ nuclei, in which the mean length:width ratio increased from ~2 to ~3.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Stroma cell nuclei (SOX10+ and TFAP2B+) showed the largest increases in mean length:width ratio with dilation, from approximately 2 to approximately 5.
source: Stroma cell nuclei (SOX10+ and TFAP2B+) showed the largest increases in the mean length:width ratio, from ~2 to ~5.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A subset of migratory neural crest cells defined by Sox10-Cre expression contribute exclusively to the stromal cell populations.
source: The data are consistent with a model in which (1) a subset of migratory neural crest cells, defined by Sox10-Cre expression, contribute exclusively to the stromal cell populations and provide all or nearly all of the stromal cell progenitors
evidence: This is inferred from lineage tracing data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Migratory neural crest cells that express Wnt1-Cre2 but not Sox10-Cre contribute the majority of the progenitors for iris PE, dilator, and sphincter 2 cells.
source: and (2) migratory neural crest cells that express Wnt1-Cre2 but not Sox10-Cre contribute the majority of the progenitors for iris PE, dilator, and sphincter 2 cells, but contribution minimally to the sphincter 1 population.
evidence: This is inferred from lineage tracing data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The vast majority of sphincter 1 cells arise either from an unlabeled neural crest population or from local ocular progenitors.
source: The vast majority of sphincter 1 cells presumably arise either from an unlabeled neural crest population or from local ocular progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the minimal labeling of sphincter 1 cells in lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Smooth muscle cells are present in multiple organs and control a wide range of physiological functions.
source: Smooth muscle cells are present in multiple organs and they control a wide range of physiological functions, including vascular tone, airway resistance, gastrointestinal (GI) motility, and pupil diameter.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge.

claim: Skeletal muscle excitation involves quantal release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction leading to activation of postsynaptic nicotinic receptors and depolarization of the muscle membrane.
source: In contrast to the unitary mode of skeletal muscle excitation – quantal release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction leading to activation of postsynaptic nicotinic receptors and depolarization of the muscle membrane
evidence: This is established knowledge about skeletal muscle physiology.

claim: Smooth muscle activation and inhibition involve multiple classes of GPCRs that activate or inhibit calcium mobilization and protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation.
source: smooth muscle activation and inhibition involve multiple classes of GPCRs that activate or inhibit calcium mobilization and protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation (Kuo and Ehrlich, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on smooth muscle physiology.

claim: Over the past 30 years, the iris PE has been studied as a potential source of cells for autologous transplantation to replace dying or dysfunctional RPE cells in individuals with age-related macular degeneration.
source: Over the past 30 years, the iris PE has been studied as a potential source of cells for autologous transplantation to replace dying or dysfunctional retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells in individuals with age-related macular degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by the clinical trial literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Human iris PE cells can be harvested from a small iridectomy sample and expanded in culture.
source: These studies were motivated by the surgical accessibility of human iris PE cells, which can be harvested from a small iridectomy sample and expanded in culture
evidence: This is supported by prior research on iris PE cell culture.

claim: The iris PE in non-mammalian vertebrates can transdifferentiate into other ocular cell types.
source: and by earlier work showing that the iris PE in non-mammalian vertebrates can transdifferentiate into other ocular cell types (Hu et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on iris PE transdifferentiation.

claim: In three clinical trials of sub-retinal transplantation of iris PE in age-related macular degeneration patients, there have been minimal complications but also minimal effect on the clinical course of the disease.
source: In three clinical trials of sub-retinal transplantation of iris PE in age-related macular degeneration patients, there have been minimal complications but also minimal effect on the clinical course of the disease (Lappas et al., 2004; Aisenbrey et al., 2006; Abe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical trial reports.

claim: The failure to significantly alter disease progression in iris PE transplantation is likely due to the failure of transplanted iris PE cells to acquire the phagocytic and other properties of RPE cells.
source: The failure to significantly alter disease progression is likely referable to the failure of the transplanted iris PE cells to acquire the phagocytic and other properties of RPE cells
evidence: This is inferred from the clinical trial outcomes and knowledge of RPE function.

claim: Iris inflammation (iritis) is one component of anterior segment uveitis, a common autoimmune condition.
source: Iris inflammation (iritis) is one component of anterior segment uveitis, a common autoimmune condition (Martin et al., 2002; Artornsombudh et al., 2014; Wakefield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: Stromal cells change their patterns of gene expression in response to inflammation and can epigenetically 'remember' prior bouts of inflammation.
source: Work in a variety of disease contexts has shown that stromal cells change their patterns of gene expression in response to inflammation and that they can epigenetically 'remember' prior bouts of inflammation (Neumann et al., 2010; Crowley et al., 2018; Mizoguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on stromal cell responses to inflammation.

claim: The chronic and relapsing/remitting character of uveitis suggests that iris stromal cells might undergo long-lasting changes in gene expression during a bout of uveitis.
source: The chronic and relapsing/remitting character of uveitis suggests that iris stromal cells might similarly undergo long-lasting changes in gene expression during a bout of uveitis (Grunwald et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the nature of uveitis and stromal cell behavior in other contexts.

claim: Multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome (MSMDS) or megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome (MMIHS) manifest in infancy with life-threatening defects in GI motility.
source: The most severe inherited disorders of smooth muscle cell function, referred to as multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome (MSMDS) or megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome (MMIHS), manifest in infancy with life-threatening defects in GI motility and are associated with mutations in the genes coding for components of the contractile machinery, including myosin light chain kinase (MYLK), SMA (ACTA2), and myosin heavy chain-11 (MYH11) (Moreno et al., 2016; Gamboa and Sood, 2019; Hashmi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: MSMDS/MMIHS are associated with mutations in genes coding for myosin light chain kinase (MYLK), SMA (ACTA2), and myosin heavy chain-11 (MYH11).
source: The most severe inherited disorders of smooth muscle cell function, referred to as multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome (MSMDS) or megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome (MMIHS), manifest in infancy with life-threatening defects in GI motility and are associated with mutations in the genes coding for components of the contractile machinery, including myosin light chain kinase (MYLK), SMA (ACTA2), and myosin heavy chain-11 (MYH11) (Moreno et al., 2016; Gamboa and Sood, 2019; Hashmi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: Defects in pupil constriction have been reported in patients with MSMDS/MMIHS.
source: Defects in pupil constriction have been reported in patients with MSMDS/MMIHS, consistent with contractile defects in iris smooth muscle (Moller et al., 2012; Roulez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical reports.

claim: Pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS) is characterized by the release of excessive quantities of cellular material, including pigment granules, from the iris PE into the aqueous humor.
source: The release into the aqueous humor of excessive quantities of cellular material, including pigment granules, from the iris PE is the hallmark of pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS) (Niyadurupola and Broadway, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: If sufficient quantities of material from iris PE become trapped in the trabecular meshwork, the resulting rise in intraocular pressure can lead to pigmentary glaucoma (PG).
source: If sufficient quantities of this material become trapped in the trabecular meshwork, the ocular drainage structure, the resulting rise in intraocular pressure can lead to a subtype of open angle glaucoma referred to as pigmentary glaucoma (PG).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the pathophysiology of pigmentary glaucoma.

claim: PDS is associated with increased contact between the iris and lens.
source: PDS is associated with increased contact between the iris and lens, which may predispose to pigment release secondary to mechanical trauma (Aptel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: In mice, mutations in melanosomal genes lead to PDS, PG, and iris stromal atrophy.
source: In mice, mutations in melanosomal genes lead to PDS, PG, and a related disorder, iris stromal atrophy (Anderson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the cited mouse genetics study.

claim: In humans, PDS has a genetic component, but the contributing genes are still largely unknown.
source: In humans, PDS also has a genetic component, but the contributing genes are still largely unknown (Tandon et al., 2019; van der Heide et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited genetic studies.

claim: Exfoliation syndrome is characterized by impaired pupil constriction and by the release of extracellular matrix material from the iris and lens.
source: A conceptually similar disorder, exfoliation syndrome, is characterized by impaired pupil constriction and by the release of extracellular matrix material from the iris and lens, which accumulates in the trabecular meshwork and can lead to open angle glaucoma (Kivelä, 2018; Schlötzer-Schrehardt, 2018; Tekin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: Exfoliation syndrome has a strong genetic component, with seven loci identified in genome-wide association studies.
source: Exfoliation syndrome has a strong genetic component, with seven loci identified in genome-wide association studies (Aboobakar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited GWAS study.

claim: Most primary iris cysts are benign and do not lead to visual disability.
source: Most primary cysts are benign and do not lead to visual disability.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Iris cysts that arise as secondary consequences of surgical or non-surgical trauma are more likely to enlarge and can lead to obstruction of vision, uveitis, or glaucoma.
source: Cysts that arise as secondary consequences of surgical or non-surgical trauma are more likely to enlarge and can lead to obstruction of vision, uveitis, or glaucoma (Shields and Shields, 2017; Georgalas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: Transcription factors PITX2 and FOXC1 are required for normal migration of peri-ocular mesenchyme cells.
source: Transcription factors PITX2 and FOXC1 are required for normal migration of peri-ocular mesenchyme cells
evidence: This is established knowledge from developmental biology studies.

claim: Mutations in PITX2 or FOXC1 produce hypoplasia of the iris stroma, holes in the iris, and an eccentric position of the pupil (Rieger anomaly).
source: and mutations in PITX2 or FOXC1 produce (1) hypoplasia of the iris stroma, holes in the iris, and an eccentric position of the pupil (Rieger anomaly)
evidence: This is established clinical and genetic knowledge.

claim: Mutations in PITX2 or FOXC1 can produce strands of ectopic tissue in the space between iris and cornea (Axenfeld anomaly).
source: and/or (2) strands of ectopic tissue in the space between iris and cornea (Axenfeld anomaly).
evidence: This is established clinical and genetic knowledge.

claim: Iris development is sensitive to reductions in PAX6 activity, with phenotypes ranging from mild iris hypoplasia to complete aniridia.
source: Iris development is also sensitive to reductions in PAX6 activity, with phenotypes ranging from mild iris hypoplasia to complete aniridia (Hingorani et al., 2012; Cvekl and Callaerts, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on PAX6 function in eye development.

claim: Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) occurs during approximately 2% of cataract surgeries.
source: An important iatrogenic disorder, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS), occurs during ~2% of cataract surgeries and is a risk factor for surgical complications (Enright et al., 2017; Christou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: IFIS is a risk factor for surgical complications during cataract surgery.
source: An important iatrogenic disorder, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS), occurs during ~2% of cataract surgeries and is a risk factor for surgical complications (Enright et al., 2017; Christou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical literature.

claim: IFIS is characterized by pupil constriction, a flacid and billowing iris, and prolapse of the iris through the surgical incision.
source: IFIS is characterized by pupil constriction, a flacid and billowing iris, and prolapse of the iris through the surgical incision.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about IFIS.

claim: IFIS is strongly linked to prior or ongoing systemic treatment with alpha1-adrenergic receptor antagonists.
source: IFIS is strongly linked to prior or ongoing systemic treatment with alpha1-adrenergic receptor antagonists, most commonly for benign prostatic hypertrophy
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Alpha1-adrenergic receptor antagonists presumably lead to long-term changes in iris smooth muscle physiology.
source: which presumably leads to long-term changes in iris smooth muscle physiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the association between alpha1-antagonist use and IFIS.

claim: The asymmetry in gene expression responses to dilation vs. constriction most likely reflects the tissue compression associated with pupil dilation.
source: The asymmetry in gene expression responses, in which an iris with a dilated pupil differs from an untreated iris but an iris with a constricted pupil is nearly identical to an untreated iris, most likely reflects the tissue compression associated with pupil dilation
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression data and mechanical changes observed with dilation.

claim: With pupil constriction, the iris is flattened to an even greater extent than it is in the untreated (resting) state.
source: By contrast, with pupil constriction, the iris is flattened to an even greater extent than it is in the untreated (resting) state.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanical changes associated with constriction.

claim: The gene expression changes observed with pupil dilation could represent physiologic adaptations to changes in metabolic state and/or cell shape.
source: The gene expression changes observed with pupil dilation could represent physiologic adaptations to changes in metabolic state and/or cell shape.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed gene expression changes.

claim: Pde10a codes for a cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase that may function to homeostatically regulate cAMP and/or cGMP signaling.
source: Consistent with this view, Pde10a, a transcript that is highly expressed in the brain and is strongly induced by dilation in iris and ciliary body cell types, codes for a cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase that may function to homeostatically regulate cAMP and/or cGMP signaling (Conti and Beavo, 2007; Wilson and Brandon, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on Pde10a function.

claim: Egr1 codes for an immediate early transcription factor that responds to a wide variety of physiologic stimuli.
source: Similarly, Egr1, one of the transcripts that is strongly induced in dilator muscle, codes for an immediate early transcription factor that responds to a wide variety of physiologic stimuli, including growth factor stimulation in many cell types and synaptic activity in neurons (Duclot and Kabbaj, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on Egr1 function.

claim: It seems plausible that iris gene expression changes might accompany the pharmacologic pupil dilation associated with routine ophthalmoscopic examinations of the human retina.
source: Extrapolating from the observations reported here to the human iris, it seems plausible that iris gene expression changes might also accompany the pharmacologic pupil dilation associated with routine ophthalmoscopic examinations of the human retina.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from mouse to human.

claim: Distortions in nuclear shape in response to mechanical stress lead to changes in transcription factor localization.
source: Changes in the force exerted on the nucleus lead to (1) changes in transcription factor localization, as seen for YAP/TAZ (Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017; Kassianidou et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on nuclear mechanobiology.

claim: Distortions in nuclear shape in response to mechanical stress lead to chromatin reorganization.
source: (2) chromatin reorganization (Miroshnikova et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on nuclear mechanobiology.

claim: Distortions in nuclear shape in response to mechanical stress lead to direct and indirect changes in gene expression.
source: (3) direct and indirect changes in gene expression (Tajik et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on nuclear mechanobiology.

claim: Distortions in nuclear shape in response to mechanical stress lead to changes in cytoskeletal organization.
source: and (4) changes in cytoskeletal organization (Hoffman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on nuclear mechanobiology.

claim: Female albino mice were used throughout this study to facilitate visualization of fluorescent antibody and in situ hybridization probes.
source: Female albino mice were used throughout this study to facilitate visualization of fluorescent antibody and in situ hybridization (ISH) probes.
evidence: This is a methodological choice stated in the manuscript.

claim: A total of 34,357 nuclei were analyzed by snRNAseq.
source: snRNAseq data were obtained from a total of 34,357 nuclei (dilation: 11,027 nuclei; constriction: 8965 nuclei; no treatment: 14,365 nuclei) with a mean of 1760 transcripts detected per nucleus, using the 10× Genomics Chromium platform (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the snRNAseq experiment.

claim: A mean of 1760 transcripts were detected per nucleus in the snRNAseq analysis.
source: snRNAseq data were obtained from a total of 34,357 nuclei (dilation: 11,027 nuclei; constriction: 8965 nuclei; no treatment: 14,365 nuclei) with a mean of 1760 transcripts detected per nucleus, using the 10× Genomics Chromium platform (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the snRNAseq experiment.

claim: Among independent replicates from mice subject to the same treatment, RNAseq read counts showed pairwise Pearson correlations of 0.98–0.99.
source: Among independent replicates from mice subject to the same treatment, RNAseq read counts showed pairwise Pearson correlations of 0.98–0.99 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Six and one-half hours was chosen as the duration for dilation or constriction to provide sufficient time for any changes in gene expression to be fully manifest.
source: Six and one-half hours was chosen as the duration for dilation or constriction to provide sufficient time for any changes in gene expression to be fully manifest.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale stated in the manuscript.
